query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (≈0.1 at.%) of boron to an equimolar HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its strength–plasticity combination by inducing the formation of fine boride precipitates at the grain boundaries that enhance cohesion without compromising the matrix strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar single-phase HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.1 at.% boron during alloy processing to promote local precipitation at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Prepared using standard metallurgical processing routes, under controlled cooling conditions that favor fine, discontinuous precipitation at the grain boundaries, and tested at both room temperature and elevated temperatures relevant to high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine hexagonal close-packed borides (likely (Hf, Zr)B2) precipitated at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The intergranular boride precipitates enhance grain boundary cohesion, preventing intergranular fracture and enabling more uniform plastic deformation by altering local stress distributions. This results in improved work hardenability and ductility while retaining adequate matrix strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (boron-free) alloy, the boron-modified alloy will exhibit markedly improved ductility and work hardening behavior, with a higher yield point and better overall strength–plasticity balance.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the original HfNbTaTiZr alloy without any boron addition.
generation.boundary: The positive effect is expected only when the boron content is optimized around 0.1 at.%; deviations (significantly lower or higher boron levels) or processing conditions that result in coarse or overly continuous precipitates may not yield the desired balance of properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nature, distribution, and long-term thermal stability of the boride precipitates under cyclic high-temperature conditions remain uncertain and may affect the reproducibility of the improved performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar HfNbTaTiZr alloys under identical processing conditions: one with 0.1 at.% boron addition and one without. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and SEM to confirm the presence and distribution of boride precipitates at the grain boundaries. Conduct mechanical tests (tensile and hardness tests) at room temperature and elevated temperatures to evaluate yield strength, ductility, and work hardening.
measurements: TEM/SEM imaging of grain boundary precipitates
Hardness measurements at grain boundaries and matrix
Tensile tests measuring yield strength and elongation
Work hardening rate from stress-strain curves
Comparative analysis of mechanical performance at elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility and work hardening (or shows inferior performance) compared to the boron-free baseline, or if the predicted boride precipitates are absent or coarsely formed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mec

For single-phase solid-solution RHEAs, although the mechanical properties may be improved by the adjustment of the compositions, the strength–ductility trade-off problem remains [], and the development of other robust RHEAs is still demanded.
In recent years, heterostructural HEAs with microstructural heterogeneity to generate plastic discontinuity and thus mechanical strengthening have been intensively developed for overcoming the strength–ductility trade-off problem [,,,]. The proposed heterostructures include multiphase (most often called complex concentrated alloys), eutectic dual-phase and single-phase (grain-size gradient) structures [,,]. Among them, the precipitation-strengthened heterostructure without the need of marked changes in the fabrication process is more efficient and can be applied to the industry more easily.
